844b30ba.title: Why proxy assessors bias disability ratings
844b30ba.takeaway: Proxies rate patients as more disabled than other measures do, so use the same respondent type at every follow-up.

points.heading: Who answers the questionnaire?
points.body: Assessments may be performed by rehabilitation providers, patients, or proxies, and their ratings can differ.

points.heading: Proxies overestimate disability
points.body: Proxy assessors tend to rate patients as more disabled than other functional measures suggest, and the gap grows with more impaired patients.
points.source: Duncan et al., 2002; Williams et al., 2006

points.heading: The frame of reference trap
points.body: Healthcare professionals tend to rate patients higher than patients rate themselves due to a difference in the frame of reference used.

references: Duncan, P. W., Lai, S. M., Tyler, D., Perera, S., Reker, D. M., & Studenski, S. (2002). Evaluation of Proxy Responses to the Stroke Impact Scale. Stroke, 33(11), 2593–2599. https://doi.org/10.1161/01.str.0000034395.06874.3e

Sneeuw, K. C., Sprangers, M. A., & Aaronson, N. K. (2002). The role of health care providers and significant others in evaluating the quality of life of patients with chronic disease. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 55(11), 1130–1143. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0895-4356(02)00479-1

Williams, L. S., Bakas, T., Brizendine, E., Plue, L., Tu, W., Hendrie, H., & Kroenke, K. (2006). How Valid Are Family Proxy Assessments of Stroke Patients’ Health-Related Quality of Life?. Stroke, 37(8), 2081–2085. https://doi.org/10.1161/01.str.0000230583.10311.9f

7bc8e19b.title: Why opaque reporting is a problem for research
7bc8e19b.takeaway: Opaque reporting is linked to biased conclusions, and without clear methods readers cannot judge whether findings are reliable.

points.heading: Opaque reporting and biased conclusions
points.body: Opaque reporting is directly associated with biased conclusions and, less directly, with errors in biomedical publishing and inefficient use of scarce resources.

points.heading: Judging reliability becomes impossible
points.body: Without knowing study methods, readers cannot determine if results are trustworthy.

references: Buccheri, R. K., & Sharifi, C. (2017). Critical Appraisal Tools and Reporting Guidelines for Evidence‐Based Practice. Worldviews on Evidence-Based Nursing, 14(6), 463–472. https://doi.org/10.1111/wvn.12258
Moher, D., Altman, D. G., Schulz, K. F., Simera, I., & Wager, E. (2014). Guidelines for reporting health research: A user’s manual.

checklist-consort-outcomes.title: Primary outcome: defined before, not after
checklist-consort-outcomes.takeaway: An outcome is prespecified only if variable, metric, aggregation and time point are written first.

points.heading: What the item asks
points.body: Report every prespecified primary and secondary outcome: measurement variable, analysis metric, method of aggregation and time point.

points.heading: Why it matters
points.body: Vague outcomes invite switching after the data are in, one of the best-documented sources of reporting bias.

points.heading: How to comply
points.body: Example: pain on a 0–10 numeric scale (variable), change from baseline (metric), mean (aggregation), at 12 weeks (time point).

references: Hopewell, S., Chan, A.-W., Collins, G. S., Hróbjartsson, A., Moher, D., Schulz, K. F., et al. (2025). CONSORT 2025 statement: Updated guideline for reporting randomised trials. BMJ, 389, e081123. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2024-081123
